German chancellor Merkel and federal state MPs support media calls for a legal ban on adblockers (full translation in comments)

The juridicial way takes to long for the media and advertisers. Now the political machine is urged to enable a ban on adblockers - with support from the big animals.

The media and the advertising industry continue their battle against adblockers and now hope for support from the political machine. In a paper released on Friday, the federal and state commission for media convergence dedicates an entire chapter to the question of how the media can protect itself against the growing use of adblockers. According to the 39-page report, a "soon examination by the federal government and the federal states will examine whether the economic and media-political risks may necessitate a legal restriction". It appears that chancellor Angela Merkel (CDU) and the prime ministers of the federal states have intervented in the debate. In December, the comission had showcased an interim report, which did not discuss the topic at all. But then political influence from the highest level seemingly made itself felt. "Following a meeting with the chancellor and the federal PMs concerning the interim report on on December 3rd, the federal and state comission for media convergence was additionally asked to also investigate the topics of media agencies and that of ad-blockers", the final report says. Stemming from this March 8th 2016 allegedly saw a workshop, in which the media and the advertising industry could make their complaints against adblockers heard. Adblock developers such as the cologne-based Eyeo GmbH were not present.

- Axel Springer faces defeat in the regional appeal court of Stuttgart -

The media argues that, that the use of adblockers is "practically tearing apart" their journalistic service. According to them, there is no "right to unpaid information, because of which one either must pay for the media product, or watch adverts". With this, the media repeats an argumentation with which it already has repeatedly lost at courts. Most recently on Thursday, at the regional appeal court of Stuttgart. There, lawyers of the Axel Springer publishing company revoked their appeal against a verdict of the regional appeal court of Stuttgart, "after the 2. civil senate has, after in-depth discussion of the respective legal issue, advised the parties that it considers the verdict of the regional appeal court to be correct". (Translators notice: The discussed case was about a Safari-based adblocker called "Blockr". Axel Springer is one of Germany's largest publishing companies).

- Paid content and arms race are no alternatives -

At the workshop, the media did not mention that they are unlikely to score a a legan ban on adblockers at court, but said that: "The waiting for a verdict from the supreme court on legal questions especially based on fair trading practices, which different courts hitherto have answered in different ways, is not considered acceptable." Furthermore, they did not consider the verdict of the federal high court of justice, according to which adblockers in television were permissible, to be non-applicable. "Switching to paid content or a technical arms race was no sustainable alternative for them", the report goes on to state. Yet the lobbyists, that are referred to as "Stakeholders", seem to contradict themselves. Even though adblockers are already seen as "against the law, they believe that there is a "legal and and media-political need for a statutory ban on adblockers". Their suggestion: "One potential option might be a form of integrity protection for journalistic-editorial digital products, similar to the idea behind the signal protection in broadcasting law." This signal protection means that a signal may not be manipulated from a third party during its way from the broadcaster to the consumer.

- Geoblocking for adblockers? -

The respective work group of the comission apparently joined into the critique. It sees the business modell of adblockers "as legaly, and, in view of the refinancing of journalistic-editorial products, also media-politically problematic. The workgroup therefore considers the "investigation of legal rules as necessary".

How such a ban on adblockers might look like remains unclear, however. Even in the future, users likely would be able to install the respective browser plug-ins. Will German users therefore face the geoblocking of browsers or addons? As the complaints of media companies such as Axel Springer seemingly have already made their way to the top of the government, this can not be ruled out. But it is equally possible that the investigation finds no means for a ban of adblockers. Next week will see a further legal clarification. For then, the regional appeal court of cologne will give its verdict on the dispute between Springer and Eyeo.
